{'role': 'user', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '<file name="D:\\dev\\ab-tasks\\_briefs\\raptor\\brief.md">\n# Task Brief: Port Raptor: Call of the Shadows (Sector 1) to HTML5\n\n## 1. Goal\n\nPort *Raptor: Call of the Shadows* (Apogee, 1994) — sector 1 only, the shareware\ncontent — from the original DOS game to a browser game built with HTML5 canvas,\nvanilla JavaScript, and the Web Audio API. The port must render real game assets\n(graphics and sounds) extracted from the original shareware data files, either at\nbuild time or at runtime — no placeholder art, no placeholder audio. Do not use\nany external frameworks or libraries beyond what ships in the browser (no React,\nPhaser, PixiJS, Howler, etc.). A small vanilla test runner is fine if you want\none, but it is not required.\n\n## 2. Worktree Layout\n\nYour worktree root (`./`) contains the GPL C/ASM source of the original DOS game,\nprovided for reference and porting purposes, under `SOURCE/`, `GFX/`, `audiolib/`,\nand `apodmx/`. It also contains the original shareware game data files under\n`./data/` — GLB archive files, the shareware `RAP.EXE` for reference, and whatever\nelse the shareware distribution contained.\n\nBuild your web port as new files alongside/above this existing tree (for example\n`index.html`, an asset-extraction or build script, and your JS source), and keep\nthe original source tree intact for reference — do not delete or rewrite it.\n\nYou must write and maintain a `README` documenting a working dev-server command\n(for example `npx serve .`, `python -m http.server`, or similar) so that the port\ncan be opened and played in a browser at any milestone. Keep this command accurate\nand working as you go — it will be used to check your progress at each milestone.\n\n## 3. Standing Rules\n\n- Vanilla JavaScript + HTML5 canvas + Web Audio API only. No external runtime\n  frameworks or libraries. A lightweight bundler or dev-only tool is fine if it\n  produces plain output, but avoid dependency-heavy tooling.\n- Always leave behind a documented, working dev server command that serves a\n  working build.\n- Commit to git after completing each milestone (M1 through M5, below), so\n  progress is checkpointed.\n- Sector 1 (shareware) content only — you do not need to support later sectors\n  or the registered/full game.\n\n## 4. Milestone Ladder (M1–M5)\n\nThis is the actual grading spec. Copied verbatim:\n\n- **M1**: level-1 background + player ship rendered on canvas from the real GLB\n  data. Graded by screenshot similarity (SSIM) to a reference DOSBox frame on the\n  playfield region (target >= 0.80), and >= 90% of the reference color palette\n  present.\n- **M2**: arrow keys move the ship; firing spawns a projectile.\n- **M3**: wave-1 enemies spawn; a projectile hit decrements enemy HP or removes\n  the enemy; the player can die.\n- **M4**: HUD (score/shields) renders; a Web Audio context is running and at\n  least one sound effect is triggered on firing.\n- **M5**: the sector-1 loop completes — the wave counter advances through wave 9\n  and a sector-complete screen appears.\n\n## 5. Grader Interface Contract\n\nYou **must** implement exactly this. An automated Playwright script checks\nagainst it — this is a hard requirement, not a suggestion.\n\n- A canvas element `<canvas id="raptor-canvas">` whose internal pixel buffer is\n  exactly 320x200 (`canvas.width === 320`, `canvas.height === 200`), independent\n  of any CSS display scaling.\n- Controls: `ArrowUp` / `ArrowDown` / `ArrowLeft` / `ArrowRight` move the ship;\n  the Space bar fires. Use standard `keydown`/`keyup` DOM listeners — no custom\n  input hook needed.\n- A live-updated global object `window.__raptor` with this exact shape:\n\n  ```js\n  window.__raptor = {\n    ready: boolean,            // true once the first frame (background + player ship) is drawn from real game data\n    player: { x: number, y: number, alive: boolean },\n    projectiles: [ { x: number, y: number, owner: \'player\'|\'enemy\' }, /* ... */ ],\n    enemies: [ { id: string|number, hp: number, x: number, y: number, alive: boolean }, /* ... */ ],\n    hud: { score: number, shields: number },\n    audio: { contextState: \'running\'|\'suspended\'|\'closed\', sfxCount: number },  // sfxCount increments on every SFX triggered\n    wave: number,               // current wave within sector 1\n    sectorComplete: boolean\n  };\n  ```\n\n- Keep this object\'s fields in sync with actual game state at all times. The\n  grader polls it, drives real keyboard input to test M2/M3/M4/M5, and takes a\n  canvas screenshot to test M1. For M5 the grader is allowed to auto-play (hold\n  fire, jitter movement) rather than requiring skilled play, so you do not need\n  to build any special "autoplay" or "god mode" feature — just make the interface\n  accurately reflect real game state during ordinary play.\n\n</file>\n'}], 'attribution': 'user', 'timestamp': 1787269449733}

LPLAYER_PIC = 0x0001011a (ITEM:282). So lship[0..6] = items 282..288.\n- `flatlib[0] = FLATSG1_ITM` (game 0 = sector 1).\n- numbers[0..10] = N0_PIC..N$_PIC (items 5..15).\n- Map items: MAP1G1..MAP9G1.\n- `startflat[0] = STARTG1TILES + 1` (item 0x1035F + 1 = 0x10360). Then each flat index `n` maps to item `startflat[0] + n`. So the flats in sector 1 are items starting at 0x10360 (ITEM:864).\n\nWait, GLB_GetItemID("STARTG1TILES") returns the label item 0x1035f. Then startflat[0]++ = 0x10360. Each map cell\'s `flats` index refers to FLATSG1 lib entry. The tile picture item = startflat[0] + flats.\n\nThe FLATSG1_ITM is a FLATS array:\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n   INT  linkflat;  // linked flat (for destroyed state)\n   SHORT bonus;    // bounty money\n   SHORT bounty;   // hits\n}FLATS;\n```\nEach entry: linkflat (INT=4 bytes), bonus (SHORT=2), bounty (SHORT=2) = 8 bytes per entry.\n\nThe map cells reference flats index. For a "no tile" / empty cell, flats is presumably 0. The first flat (index 0) after STARTG1TILES is item 0x10360 which should be the "empty/sky" background tile.\n\nOK. Now let me look at the game flow. The game is: WIN_MainMenu → WIN_MainLoop. That involves menus. But for the port, we don\'t need full menus — we need to directly start sector 1 wave 1, run the loop, and detect sector complete.\n\nFor M5: "the sector-1 loop completes — the wave counter advances through wave 9 and a sector-complete screen appears." Except for\nthe aforementioned garbage data, this one should perfectly match.\n\nThe originally released AUDIO.MAK file was used as a base, albeit with minor\ninfluences from AUDIO2.MAK (as available with the released ROTT sources).\nYou shall *not* call "wmake" on your own anymore. Instead, use BUILD.BAT.\n\nList of releases by LIB/directory file names\n--------------------------------------------\n\n- AL950724: Apogee Sound System v1.04 (imperfect as stated above).\n- AL_109: Apogee Sound System v1.09 (with one bit of imperfection).\n- AL_11: Apogee Sound System v1.1.\n\nHow to identify code changes (and what\'s this ASSREV thing)?\n------------------------------------------------------------\n\nDifferent values of LIBVER_ASSREV are defined for differing builds of the\nlibrary. It is intended to represent a revision of development of\nthe Apogee Sound System codebase. Usually, this revision value is based\non some *guessed* date (e.g., an original modification date of the LIB),\nbut this does not have to be the case.\n\nNote that only C sources (and not ASM) are covered by the above for now.\n\nVia AUDIO.MAK, Watcom Make (wmake) manually sets LIBVER_ASSREV\nto the desired LIB file revision string.\n\nThese are two good reasons for using ASSREV as described above, referring\nto similar work done for Wolfenstein 3D EXEs (built with Borland C++):\n\n- WL1AP12 and WL6AP11 share the same code revision. However, WL1AP11\nis of an earlier revision. Thus, the usage of WOLFREV can be\nless confusing.\n- WOLFREV is a good way to describe the early March 1992 build. While\nit\'s commonly called just "alpha" or "beta", GAMEVER_WOLFREV\ngives us a more explicit description.\n\nWhat is this based on\n---------------------\n\nThis codebase is based on the Apogee Sound System sources as originally\nreleased by Apogee Software, Ltd. (DBA 3D Realms) on 2002, along with\nthe Rise of the Triad sources. It still depends on additional\nbinary LIB files, being GF1_OSF.LIB and PAWE32.LIB.\n\nHow was the makefile (and a bit more) modified from the original\n----------------------------------------------------------------\n\n- The codebase was originally modified for ROTT, Apogee v1.3. This covers\nwhat is guessed to be Apogee Sound System v1.04. As in AUDIO2.MAK from\nthe released sources, ADLIBFX.OBJ and PCFX.OBJ are now dependencies for\nv1.04. In addition, BLASTOLD.OBJ is a dependency instead of BLASTER.OBJ.\nMV_MIX5.OBJ is another dependency, while MV_MIX.OBJ and MV_MIX16.OBJ\nare *not*. As in the released AUDIO.MAK file (rather than AUDIO2.MAK),\nMVREVERB.OBJ is *still* a dependency, too. Finally, AUDIO.MAK was\nmodified so the library, as well as the new objects files, are\ncreated in a separate directory, depending on the version.\n- Various source code files were modified. As hinted above, BLASTOLD.C is\nnow used instead of BLASTER.C for v1.04 (although BLASTER.H is still used).\n- Recreated code of v1.1 (as used in Duke Nukem 3D: Atomic Edition 1.4-1.5)\nwas added later, somewhat more similar to 1.12 as released on 2002.\n- Even later, 1.09 (matching Shadow Warrior 1.0-1.2) was added. Since almost\nall changes were already applied during the (partial) recreation of 1.04,\nthis mostly covered changes to compared LIBVER_ASSREV values.\nAdditional checks related to GUS were added, though. A few bits of debugging\ninformation were used in order to further improve the accuracy, even if\nnot by much. This comes to adding \'#include "memcheck.h"\' to a bunch\nof C files, and similarly replacing "interrup.h" with "interrupt.h".\n- There may be at least one other difference.\n\nBuilding each LIB\n=================\n\nRequired tools:\n\n- Watcom C 10.0b (and no other version).\n- Turbo Assembler v3.1 (from Borland C++ 3.1).\n\nNotes before trying to build anything:\n\n- This may depend on luck. In fact, as of now, it *is* known that you\'ll get\na different LIB, although it should be equivalent in behaviors in the cases of\nversions 1.09 & 1.1 (and identical for 1.1 up to misc. Watcom-generated data).\n- Even if code is perfectly matching, the OBJ/LIB files will\nstill include data like original paths and timestamps of\nsource files (including local or system headers).\n- Use BUILD.BAT to build the library (don\'t call wmake directly),\nor CLEAN.BAT to remove the library and created object files.\n\nFor reference, a list of such original paths in use is given here:\n- System headers: c:\\ln\\watcom\\h.\n- Apogee Sound System source dir: C:\\PRG\\AUDIO\\source for version 1.04,\nD:\\PRG\\AUDIO\\source for 1.09 and 1.1.\n\nBuilding the LIB\n----------------\n\n1. Use BUILD.BAT, passing the corresponding LIB identifier\n(the output LIB filename without the .LIB extension) as an argument.\n2. Hopefully you should get a LIB that *behaves close to the original*,\nbut do *not* expect it to be identical.\n\nKnown issues\n------------\n\nThere are known differences in the output that should be listed,\ncompared to AUDIOLIB 1.04 (as a part of ROTT 1.3):\n- Small differences in FX_SetupCard and FX_Init from FX_MAN.C.\n- Larger differences in MULTIVOC.C:MV_ServiceVoc. In fact, this is been the\n*most* problematic part for now. The function body\'s length is even different\nfrom the original. There\'s a little bit of a HACK that can be used to force\nthe original length (look for an instance of "#if 0"), but remember this:\nBy enabling the hack, you MODIFY the behaviors of MV_ServiceVoc!\nFrom AUDIOLIB and ROTT:\n- Misc. global variables found in locations differing from the originals\nin the recreated ROTT EXE layout.\n\nFor 1.09 (used in SW 1.0-1.2), there\'s still a minor difference in\nFX_SetupCard, but it shouldn\'t have an impact on the behaviors.\n\nWith 1.1 (Duke3D 1.4-1.5), the generated code should essentially be identical.\n\nFurthermore, most chances are that paddings between string literals, or\npossibly less commonly between global variables, will be filled with different\nvalues. if ( gcnt & 1 )\r\n      {\r\n         cur->pos++;\r\n\r\n         if ( cur->pos >= 16 )\r\n            cur->pos = 0;\r\n\r\n         cur->curframe++;\r\n\r\n         if ( cur->curframe >= {\r\n               cur->dflag  = TRUE;\r\n               cur->countdown = 50;\r\n            }\r\n            else\r\n            {\r\n               cur = BONUS_Remove ( cur );\r\n buf.length);\n  out.set(buf instanceof Uint8Array ? buf : new Uint8Array(buf));\n  let prev = SERIAL.charCodeAt(KIDX0);\n  let kidx = KIDX0;\n  for (let i = 0; i < out.length; i++) {\n    const byte = out[i];\n    let d = (byte - SERIAL.charCodeAt(kidx) - prev) % 256;\n    if (d < 0) d += 256;\n    out[i] = d;\n    prev = byte;\n    kidx = (kidx + 1) % KLEN;\n  }\n  return out;\n}\n\nconst dv = (b, o) => new DataView(b.buffer, b.byteOffset + o, b.byteLength - o);\n\nexport class GLBFile {\n  // `data` is an ArrayBuffer of the whole .GLB file.\n  constructor(data) {\n    this.data = data;\n    const head = decrypt(new Uint8Array(data, 0, 28));\n    this.count = dv(head, 4).getUint32(0, true);\n    this.items = [];\n    const idt = new Uint8Array(data);\n    for (let i = 0; i < this.count; i++) {\n      const e = decrypt(idt.subarray(28 + i * 28, 28 + (i + 1) * 28));\n      const v = dv(e, 0);\n      this.items.push({\n        index: i,\n        opt: v.getUint32(0, true),\n        offset: v.getUint32(4, true),\n        filesize: v.getUint32(8, true),\n        name: String.fromCharCode(...e.subarray(12, 28)).split(\'\\0\')[0],\n      });\n    }\n    this._byName = new Map();\n    for (const it of this.items) this._byName.set(it.name, it);\n  }\n\n  itemSize(nameOrIndex) {\n    const it = typeof nameOrIndex === \'number\' ?   "summary": "## Goal\nPort *Raptor: Call of the Shadows* (Apogee 1994, shareware sector 1 only) to a browser game using HTML5 canvas, vanilla JavaScript, and Web Audio API \u2014 no external frameworks. Graded against 5 milestones (M1\u2013M5) with a strict Playwright grader contract.\n\n## Constraints & Preferences\n- Vanilla JS + canvas + Web Audio only. No React/Phaser/PixiJS/Howler, no runtime libraries.\n- Must render real GLB assets \u2014 no placeholder art/audio.\n- Original source tree under `SOURCE/`, `GFX/`, `audiolib/`, `apodmx/`, `data/` must remain intact. Build web port as new files alongside.\n- Must maintain a working, documented dev-server command in README.\n- Commit to git after each milestone.\n- Grader hard contract: `<canvas id=\"raptor-canvas\">` with `canvas.width===320 && canvas.height===200`; Arrow keys move ship, Space fires; `window.__raptor` global with exact shape `{ready, player:{x,y,alive}, projectiles:[{x,y,owner}], enemies:[{id,hp,x,y,alive}], hud:{score,shields}, audio:{contextState,sfxCount}, wave, sectorComplete}`; kept in sync with real state at all times.\n\n## Progress\n\n### Done\n- [x] Researched the entire C/ASM source architecture and all data formats needed for the port.\n- [x] Decoded GLB format empirically (verified with Node scripts):\n  - KEYFILE: `{DWORD opt, DWORD offset, DWORD filesize, CHAR name[16]}`; first KEYFILE's `offset` = item count; IDT follows at byte 28.\n  - Decryption: per-entry chained cipher, key `\"32768GLB\"`, `SEED=0x19`, starting `kidx=SEED%8=1`, `prev=key[1]`; per-entry: `d=(byte-key[kidx]-prev)%256` (add 256 if negative), `prev=original byte`. (Verified per-entry, NOT block-chained, despite code reading blocks \u2014 block chaining produced garbage; per-entry decrypt yields correct nam

{'role': 'assistant', 'content': [{'type': 'thinking', 'thinking': 'The shooting logic is important. `shoot_on` gates the whole thing. And `shoot_on` is set when countdown < 1. countdown starts at `curlib->countdown + -new->move.y` = 0 - (enemy_y). Enemy starts at y≈-150, so countdown starts ≈150. It decrements by movespeed (2/frame) → takes 75 frames before the enemy can shoot. That means enemies only start shooting ~75 frames after entering. OK.\n\nThe shooting: `shootagain = NORM_SHOOT`, `shootcount = shootcnt (1)`, `shootflag = shootstart (0)`. When shoot_on: shootflag-- → -1 → fire all guns, shootflag=shotspace(4), shootcount-- → 0 → shootagain = shootframe(20). Then 20 frames of no fire (shootagain--), then shootagain=START_SHOOT → reset shootcount=1, shootflag=4 → NORM_SHOOT again. So pattern: fire burst of 1 shot (shootcount=1), wait 20 frames, fire again, wait 20... So effectively fires every ~25 frames per enemy. Much slower than I feared (I misread — shootagain gates between bursts).\n\nLet me verify MY engine implements this shootagain logic correctly. Let me check my enemyThink shoot_on handling.', 'thinkingSignature': 'reasoning'}, {'type': 'toolCall', 'id': 'chatcmpl-tool-8c0be8ffa4d56621', 'name': 'read', 'arguments': {'path': 'D:/dev/ab-tasks/raptor-dsv4/js/engine.js:960-995', 'i': 'Checking my shoot logic'}, 'partialArgs': '{"path": "D:/dev/ab-tasks/raptor-dsv4/js/engine.js:960-995", "i": "Checking my shoot logic"}', 'streamIndex': 0, 'intent': 'Checking my shoot logic'}], 'api': 'openai-completions', 'provider': 'pod-dsv4', 'model': 'deepseek-v4-flash-0731', 'usage': {'input': 49373, 'output': 382, 'cacheRead': 0, 'cacheWrite': 0, 'totalTokens': 49755, 'cost': {'input': 0, 'output': 0, 'cacheRead': 0, 'cacheWrite': 0, 'total': 0}}, 'stopReason': 'toolUse', 'timestamp': 1787270319816, 'responseId': 'chatcmpl-888782e2eb8b6420', 'duration': 2375.8064000000013, 'ttft': 505.14139999996405, 'contextSnapshot': {'promptTokens': 49373, 'nonMessageTokens': 5716}}

si--; continue; }\n      // hit test\n      if (this.enemyDamageAll(s.x, s.y, 1)) {\n        if (this.rand.random(2)) this.startAnim(A_BLUE_SPARK, s.x, s.y);\n        else this.startAnim(A_ORANGE_SPARK, s.x, s.y);\n        this.shots.splice(si, 1);
